title: The Imitation of Christ
hook: Thomas à Kempis's little book, read by Catholics and Protestants for five centuries

segments.voice: Yesterday, Catherine Benincasa, who nursed the dying and wrote to popes. Your line was be who God meant you to be. Did you speak up, gently? Day two hundred seventy-five.
screen: `BE WHO GOD MEANT YOU TO BE.`

segments.voice: Some books sit on a shelf and look important. Others get carried around until the spine cracks and the pages go soft. There's a small book, written in the Netherlands in the early 1400s, that has been that second kind for nearly six hundred years. Soldiers carried it. Prisoners read it in their cells. Catholic saints knew it almost by heart, and a founder of Methodism published his own edition of it. It has been translated into more languages than almost any book besides the Bible. And its author didn't even put his name on it. Today: ama nesciri.
screen: `A SPINE CRACKED FROM USE.` → `SOLDIERS, PRISONERS, SAINTS.` → `NO NAME ON IT.`

segments.voice: The author was almost certainly Thomas à Kempis, a quiet monk who lived most of his long life in a small community near Zwolle, in what's now the Netherlands. He spent years copying manuscripts, including the whole Bible by hand, more than once. He belonged to a movement called the Modern Devotion, ordinary believers and religious communities who wanted a simple, heartfelt, practical faith. Not arguments. Life. The book opens with a line of Jesus from John's Gospel, in the King James Bible: "he that followeth me shall not walk in darkness." And then it asks, in effect: so, are you following? Not studying him. Following. It's full of short, sharp sentences. One says, roughly, that it's better to feel sorrow for your wrongs than to know how to define the word. Another says that on the day of judgment we won't be asked what we read, but how we lived. And one of its most famous lines is just two words in Latin: ama nesciri. Love to be unknown. Don't need to be seen. Do the good thing and let no one notice. Fittingly, Thomas never signed it. The book traveled for years without an author's name, and people argued over who wrote it. That's following quietly. Remarkably, it crossed every line the churches drew. Catholics treasure it. John Wesley, one of the founders of Methodism, put out his own English version. Many Protestants read it too, and so do some Orthodox Christians, though Orthodox writers have been more divided about it. Five centuries of Christians who disagreed about a great deal have agreed on this little book: the point is to walk the way he walked, quietly, every day.
screen: `A QUIET MONK NEAR ZWOLLE.` · `HE THAT FOLLOWETH ME.` · `AMA NESCIRI: LOVE TO BE UNKNOWN.` · `READ ACROSS EVERY CHURCH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read one line, or hear one. The Imitation is often read a sentence at a time. Take this one: love to be unknown. Settle, and breathe. Let it sit. Think of something good you did recently that you wanted someone to notice. Just notice the wanting, without judging it. Then imagine doing something good today that nobody will ever find out about. How does that feel? The bell holds the time.
Ama nesciri. Latin for love to be unknown: Thomas à Kempis's own two words for doing good and letting no one notice.
Your line: follow quietly. Today, do one good thing no one will ever know about. Don't mention it. Not even later. Day two hundred seventy-five.

howItsDone: Many Christians, Catholic and Protestant above all, read The Imitation of Christ a few lines a day, often as part of morning or evening prayer.

fork.setup: you're a monk. you've written a little book that will be read for centuries. what do you do with your name?
options: put it in large letters on the first page.
fork.reveal: the book circulated without a name, and people argued for years over who wrote it. ama nesciri: love to be unknown.

original.note: Latin: love to be unknown; one of the Imitation's most famous lines.

trapdoor: what you thought: an old devotional book for monks.
what it means: a practical guide to following Jesus quietly, loved across every church for five centuries.
what a scholar hears: the Devotio Moderna; a long authorship dispute, now mostly settled on Thomas; and a copyist monk who wrote out the whole Bible by hand.

sources.quoted: he that followeth me shall not walk in darkness

sources.ref: Thomas à Kempis, The Imitation of Christ, I.1–3

notes: Imitation I.1 (contrition vs definition), I.3 (judgment: not what we read but how we lived), and I.2 ('ama nesciri et pro nihilo reputari') are paraphrased; confirm book/chapter numbers.
'Translated into more languages than almost any book besides the Bible' is a common claim; confirm wording.
John Wesley's edition: The Christian's Pattern (1735). Confirm.
Thomas copying the whole Bible by hand (the Codex of Thomas à Kempis) more than once: confirm.

Audit (wider sample): 'ama nesciri' was called three words (it is two); the claim that Orthodox Christians read it alongside Catholics and Protestants was softened, since some Orthodox writers (e.g. Ignatius Brianchaninov) criticized the book.
